newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong forwards widen but dollar seen stable.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong forwards widen but dollar seen stable.

text.p: Hong Kong dollar forwards have widened sharply in anticipation of the territory's July 1 return to Chinese rule, but experts described the activity as expected and said the dollar looks steady heading into the handover.
"There is a very low probability of any fireworks," said Eric Nickerson, currency analyst with Bank of America.
"The fact you're seeing this in the forwards, well, it's about as much as you're going to see. I don't think there will be much activity in the spot."
Three-month and six-month Hong Kong dollar forwards were trading at 135 and 240 respectively, sharply higher than the rates of 13 and 40 recorded a couple of months ago.

The wider spreads reflect an increased demand for Hong Kong dollars in the future, with dealers agreeing to buy or sell a certain amount of currency at an agreed-upon rate in order to guarantee future supply.

If speculators attack the Hong Kong dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) could be forced to step in and raise interest rates, making it prohibitively expensive for anybody to borrow in Hong Kong dollars.
While this tactic deters the speculators, it also hurts anybody who needs Hong Kong dollars to conduct business.

The increased demand for currency forwards have put pressure on interest rates, widening spreads to comparable U.S. paper and indicating rising nervousness in the market as the handover approaches, analysts said.

"It's in anticipation of anything that might happen with the handover," said Meryl Phang at MMS International. "But right now it's all reflected in the market. Things have more or less stabilised at these levels."
Little movement is expected in the spot, or cash, market with the Hong Kong dollar trading at HK$7.7414 to the U.S. dollar.
The Hong Kong currency is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar and intervention by the HKMA is not expected unless the unit reaches above HK$7.7500, experts said.

"We don't expect any major change in the exchange rate. It's still stable and while there may be some adjustment in the forward rates and interest rates, it should be enough to keep things stable," said Raj Tiwari, currency analyst with Trendsetter Financial Services.

Nickerson said recent combined central bank intervention in Asia to defend the Thai baht would act as a powerful disincentive to hedge funds contemplating an attack upon the Hong Kong dollar, as would Hong Kong and China's foreign exchange reserves.
"Right now, I would think the Hong Kong dollar would look like an unattractive currency to go after," Nickerson said.
Hong Kong held US$63.6 billion in foreign exchange reserves at the end of April, and also has a commitment of support from China, which holds US$115 billion in foreign exchange reserves.
Given the powerful external disincentives, the major risk to Hong Kong's currency stability comes not from outside but from within, said Dong Tao, senior regional economist at Schroder Securities.
"Should something externally trigger a crisis, Hong Kong dollar depositors could switch to foreign currency and there might be some trouble," Tao said.

Hong Kong people keep much of their average savings rate of 37 percent in retail bank deposits, all of which can be switched into foreign exchange at the touch of a button at automatic cash machines throughout the territory.
Analysts declined to speculate on what sort of external shock would trigger this type of capital flight, which would far exceed the HKMA's resources.
"For the time being I don't see this happening," said Tao.
